# Results -- Study 130 (Vol-Risk-Premium) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Sources: Yahoo Finance
`^VIX` (CBOE Volatility Index) and `SPY` daily closes. The VRP is computed as
`VIX - RV` where `RV = std(SPY log-ret[-21 days], ddof=1) * sqrt(252) * 100`, placing
both series in annualised-percent units. As-of **2026-06-14**.*

## Data stamp

| Series | Window | n rows | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| ^VIX + SPY daily | 1993-03-02 .. 2026-06-12 | 8,379 | `5fb9df8cc0a3` |

The VIX starts in January 1990 but SPY launched January 1993; the overlap beginning
March 1993 is the common window (after the 21-day RV warmup). The ~33-year span
covers multiple vol regimes: the Dot-Com crash, the 2008 GFC, the 2010/2011 Euro crisis,
COVID-19 (March 2020 VIX spike to 82.7), and the 2022 rates shock.

## 1. The premium -- VIX systematically exceeds trailing realised vol

The most basic question: is IV > RV on average?

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean VIX (ann. pct) | **19.53** |
| Mean 21d RV (ann. pct) | **15.85** |
| **Mean VRP = VIX − RV** | **+3.68 pp** |
| Std of VRP | 5.02 pp |
| % of days VRP > 0 | **85.7%** |
| **HAC t-stat (H0: mean VRP = 0)** | **+22.95** |

The variance risk premium is statistically overwhelming: t = 22.95 on n = 8,379 daily
observations. Option sellers collect a gross premium of ~3.7 annualised percentage points
on average; the VIX exceeds trailing RV on **86%** of days. This is the most
well-documented stylised fact in derivatives research.

## 2. Does the VRP predict forward SPY returns?

The claim is that a *high* VRP (large IV-RV spread) signals a calm, risk-on environment
and predicts *positive* forward SPY returns. We test with quintile-sorted forward returns
(rolling 252-day rank, strictly out-of-sample) at three horizons.

### Quintile-sorted 1-day forward returns

| VRP quintile | n | mean (bps) | std (bps) | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Q1 (lowest VRP) | 1,736 | +1.3 | 137.3 | +0.41 |
| Q2 | 1,527 | +3.2 | 104.7 | +1.23 |
| Q3 | 1,648 | +2.4 | 103.3 | +0.94 |
| Q4 | 1,607 | +4.9 | 101.7 | +1.99 |
| **Q5 (highest VRP)** | **1,798** | **+8.3** | **131.3** | **+2.94** |

### Q5 minus Q1 spread (the decisive test)

| Horizon | Spread (bps) | HAC t-spread | t Q5 | t Q1 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 day | +7.0 | +1.67 | +2.94 | +0.41 |
| 5 days | +16.5 | +1.11 | +3.85 | +1.72 |
| 21 days | +58.6 | +1.51 | +5.67 | +2.72 |

**Interpretation:**
- Q5 (high-VRP) days show significantly positive forward returns at all horizons
  (t ≥ 2.94 at h=1, t = 5.67 at h=21): **the top quintile has real signal**.
- However, Q1 (low-VRP) days also earn positive returns (t = 2.72 at h=21),
  weakening the *relative* signal.
- The Q5-Q1 spread does **not** clear the |t| ≥ 2 inference bar at any horizon:
  the spread t-stats are 1.67 / 1.11 / 1.51 — the return is signed correctly but
  not statistically decisive relative to the risk the test faces (overlapping returns,
  heteroskedasticity). This is a **MIXED** verdict: a single-leg signal (Q5 alone) is
  real; the spread is noisy.

## 3. Timing overlay (binary signal: long SPY when VRP > rolling median)

| Arm | Ann. Sharpe | Mean (bps/day) | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Passive buy-and-hold | 0.55 | +4.1 | +3.64 |
| Timer active (0 cost) | 0.50 | +2.6 | +3.31 |
| Timer active (1 bp cost) | 0.48 | +2.5 | +3.16 |
| **Spread (active − passive)** | — | **−1.5** | **−1.69** |

The timer (long SPY only when VRP exceeds its rolling median) **underperforms** a naive
buy-and-hold with Sharpe 0.50 vs 0.55 and a spread of −1.5 bps/day (t = −1.69, not
quite significant but consistently negative). The VRP filter *excludes* some of the best
equity days (low-VRP stress periods can suddenly resolve with sharp gains). Tradability is
**FRAGILE** by the desk's standard: the timing signal does not improve over the baseline.

## 4. Short-vol payoff distribution

Approximate stylised payoff of selling volatility on 21-day non-overlapping periods:

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| n periods | 398 |
| Mean return | +0.86% |
| Std of return | 4.43% |
| **Skew** | **−0.73** |
| Excess kurtosis | 2.64 |
| % of negative periods | 36.2% |
| 5th percentile return | −6.6% |
| **Worst period** | **−19.7%** |

The short-vol payoff has the well-documented negative skew and fat left tail: ~36% of
21-day periods are negative and the 5th percentile loss is −6.6%. The worst single period
(COVID-19 March 2020) produced a −19.7% drawdown. This quantifies the structural
"picking up nickels in front of a steamroller" nature of the trade: positive mean, but
severe right-to-left skew during vol spikes.

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** The VRP premium itself is statistically overwhelming (t = 22.95),
  confirming that IV systematically exceeds RV — the variance risk premium exists. The
  Q5 (high-VRP) quintile shows significantly positive forward returns (t = 2.94 at h=1,
  t = 5.67 at h=21). However, the Q5−Q1 spread does not clear |t| ≥ 2 at any horizon
  (max t = 1.67), and the timing overlay underperforms buy-and-hold: the VRP is REAL as
  a premium, WEAK as an equity timing signal. MIXED overall.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** The timing overlay underperforms the buy-and-hold baseline
  (Sharpe 0.50 vs 0.55, spread t = −1.69). Harvesting the actual variance premium
  requires short-options infrastructure; the payoff distribution is negatively skewed
  (skew = −0.73, worst 21-day period = −19.7%), imposing crash risk that makes the edge
  fragile in practice. A tail-hedged short-vol book can work but requires significant
  risk management overhead.
